title: Antidepressants and serotonin syndrome
blurb: Know the antidepressant classes, review people at the right time, and tell serotonin toxicity from NMS and hyponatraemia.
question: Callum, 21, was started on sertraline today for moderate depression. He asks when he will next be seen and what to look out for. What is the best answer?

teach.body: Antidepressants include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs, such as sertraline, citalopram, fluoxetine), serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs, such as venlafaxine, duloxetine), tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs, such as amitriptyline) and monoamine-oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs). SSRIs are usually first choice: they are better tolerated and safer in overdose than other classes. In plain English: SSRIs are the everyday option; TCAs and MAOIs need more caution.

teach.caption: NG222 1.4.23: do not routinely start TCAs (except lofepramine) in people at significant risk of suicide.

items.label: Review if aged 18-25 or suicide concern
Effect usually seen if it will work

teach.body: In the first few weeks there is an increased potential for agitation, anxiety and suicidal thoughts. For people aged 18 to 25 or at increased suicide risk, NICE says assess mood before prescribing, put a risk management strategy in place, review 1 week after starting or increasing the dose, and again no later than 4 weeks. Tell everyone that benefit usually appears within 4 weeks, so they do not stop too soon.

Serotonin toxicity (including serotonin syndrome) is caused by too much serotonin activity. It can appear within hours of starting or increasing a serotonergic drug, adding a second one, or switching without a long enough washout. Severe cases usually involve combinations, often including an MAOI. Treatment: stop the serotonergic drugs, give supportive care and seek specialist advice; it usually settles within about 24 hours once the drugs are stopped.

head: Feature
Serotonin toxicity
NMS
teach.caption: Both are medical emergencies: stop the causative drug and get urgent medical care.

teach.body: Nurse Hughes tells Callum that, because he is 21, he will be reviewed in 1 week, not the usual 2, and that benefit usually shows within 4 weeks. She warns him he may feel more anxious or restless at first and that suicidal thoughts can increase early on: if they do, he should get help straight away. She gives crisis numbers, mentions withdrawal if he stops suddenly, and advises him not to take St John's Wort.

teach.text: An older person on an SSRI who becomes drowsy or confused may have hyponatraemia, not worsening depression or dementia: check sodium (BNF). And St John's Wort is not a harmless add-on: NICE says do not prescribe or advise it, because of serious interactions.

items: SSRIs are usually first choice; TCAs carry the greatest overdose risk.
Review within 2 weeks; at 1 week if aged 18-25 or at particular suicide risk.
Effects usually within 4 weeks; continue at least 6 months after remission.
Serotonin toxicity: neuromuscular, autonomic and mental state changes within hours; stop drugs and get help.
Drowsiness, confusion or seizures on an antidepressant: consider hyponatraemia.

summary: You can now compare antidepressant classes, time early reviews and recognise early-treatment risks. You can tell serotonin toxicity from NMS and spot hyponatraemia.

A.q: Why are SSRIs usually chosen before tricyclic antidepressants?
options: They work within the first few days of use
They need no follow-up review after starting
They are better tolerated and safer in overdose
They cause no withdrawal symptoms when stopped
A.why: BNF: SSRIs are better tolerated and safer in overdose than other classes; NG222 1.4.23 notes TCAs carry the greatest overdose risk.

whyNot.0: Effects usually take up to 4 weeks for any class.
whyNot.1: Every new antidepressant needs early review.

A.q: Within what time is the first review usually arranged for an adult aged 40 starting an antidepressant, with no particular suicide concern?
A.why: NG222: the first review is usually within 2 weeks; it is at 1 week for people aged 18 to 25 or with particular suicide concern.

whyNot.0: One week applies to people aged 18 to 25 or at particular risk.
whyNot.2: Six weeks is too late to check early side effects and risk.
whyNot.3: Three months leaves early risks unmonitored.

A.q: Which group of features is typical of serotonin toxicity?
A.why: BNF: serotonin toxicity combines neuromuscular (clonus, hyperreflexia), autonomic (hyperthermia, sweating, diarrhoea) and mental state (agitation, confusion) changes.

whyNot.0: These do not match the autonomic overactivity of serotonin toxicity.

B.q: Nadia, 23, starts citalopram for depression. When should her first review take place?
B.why: NG222 1.4.22: people aged 18 to 25 are reviewed 1 week after starting an antidepressant or increasing the dose, because of possible early increases in suicidal thoughts.

whyNot.1: Two weeks is the usual review for adults outside the higher-risk groups.
whyNot.2: Four weeks is the latest point for a further review, not the first.
whyNot.3: Six weeks is too late for this age group.

B.q: Edna, 81, started sertraline 3 weeks ago and also takes a diuretic. Her daughter reports she is newly drowsy and confused. Which investigation is most important?
B.why: BNF and NG222 1.4.24: hyponatraemia is linked to all antidepressants, more often SSRIs, especially in older people and with diuretics; consider it with drowsiness, confusion or convulsions.

whyNot.0: Thyroid problems are possible but not the leading SSRI-related cause here.
whyNot.2: An FBC does not identify hyponatraemia.
whyNot.3: Sertraline levels are not routinely measured and would not explain this.

B.q: Sean, 35, takes an MAOI. What should the nurse include in his education?
options: Take St John's Wort to boost the effect
B.why: BNF: MAOIs have dangerous interactions with some foods and drugs and are reserved for specialist use, so dietary and medicines advice is essential.

whyNot.0: Paracetamol is not the key MAOI interaction.
whyNot.1: St John's Wort has serious interactions and is not advised (NG222).
whyNot.2: MAOI response may be delayed 3 weeks or more (BNF).

C.q: Priya, 30, takes fluoxetine. Yesterday tramadol was added for back pain. She is now agitated, sweating, shivering and has jerking movements in her legs with brisk reflexes; temperature 38.6 C. What is the most likely cause and first action?
options: NMS: stop fluoxetine and give paracetamol
Anxiety: give PRN lorazepam and recheck
Serotonin toxicity: stop both, get urgent help
Infection: take blood cultures and continue both
C.why: Rapid onset after adding a serotonergic drug, with clonus, hyperreflexia, fever and agitation, fits serotonin toxicity. Stop the serotonergic drugs and get urgent medical care (BNF).

whyNot.0: NMS follows antipsychotics, develops slowly and causes rigidity with reduced reflexes.
whyNot.1: Treating it as anxiety delays care of a medical emergency.
whyNot.3: Continuing both drugs would worsen serotonin toxicity.

C.q: Tom, 44, has depression and has taken an overdose before. His GP considers starting amitriptyline. What should the mental health nurse advise?
options: TCAs carry the greatest overdose risk
TCAs are the safest choice in overdose
TCAs need a 1-week washout from SSRIs
TCAs are preferred if sleep is poor
C.why: NG222 1.4.23: take toxicity in overdose into account; do not routinely start TCAs (except lofepramine) in people at significant risk of suicide.

whyNot.1: TCAs are the most dangerous class in overdose.
whyNot.2: Washout is not the issue; overdose toxicity is.
whyNot.3: Poor sleep does not outweigh overdose risk in someone at significant suicide risk.

C.q: Grace, 52, has taken sertraline for 7 months and feels well after a depressive episode that remitted 2 months ago. She asks if she can stop now. What is the best response?
options: Stop today, as she has been well for 2 months
Continue at least 6 months after remission
Halve the dose now and stop next week
Continue for life to prevent any relapse
C.why: BNF: continue antidepressant treatment for at least 6 months after remission; when it is stopped, reduce gradually with the prescriber.

whyNot.0: Two months is shorter than the recommended period after remission.
whyNot.2: This is both too early and too fast a reduction.
whyNot.3: Lifelong treatment is not the default; it depends on relapse risk and choice.

reteach.title: Start safely, watch closely
reteach.question: What matters most in the first weeks of an antidepressant?

blocks.body: Review within 2 weeks, or at 1 week for people aged 18 to 25 or at particular suicide risk. Warn about early agitation and suicidal thoughts. If a second serotonergic drug is added and the person becomes hot, sweaty, agitated and twitchy within hours, think serotonin toxicity.

blocks.text: Clonus and brisk reflexes point to serotonin toxicity; rigidity with slow reflexes points to NMS.

explain.body: SSRIs are better tolerated and safer in overdose. TCAs (except lofepramine) carry the greatest overdose risk and are not routinely started in people at significant suicide risk. MAOIs are specialist drugs with food and drug interactions.

test.q: Which antidepressant class carries the greatest risk in overdose?
test.why: NG222 1.4.23: TCAs (except lofepramine) are associated with the greatest risk in overdose.

whyNot.0: SSRIs are safer in overdose than other classes.
whyNot.1: SNRIs are not the class NICE names as highest risk.
whyNot.3: Mirtazapine is not the class NICE singles out.

explain.body: Usual first review within 2 weeks. For people aged 18 to 25 or at increased suicide risk: assess before prescribing, review at 1 week after starting or a dose increase, then no later than 4 weeks.

test.q: Jake, 19, has his fluoxetine dose increased. When should he be reviewed for suicidality?
test.why: NG222 1.4.22 covers people aged 18 to 25: review 1 week after starting or increasing the dose. At 19, Jake is in that group.

whyNot.0: Four weeks is the latest further review, not the first.
whyNot.1: Two weeks is the usual review for older adults without extra risk.
whyNot.2: Six weeks is too late for this age group.

explain.body: Onset within hours of a new, increased or added serotonergic drug, or a switch without washout. Neuromuscular, autonomic and mental state features. Stop the drugs, supportive care, specialist advice.

test.q: How quickly can serotonin toxicity develop after a serotonergic drug is added?
test.why: BNF: toxicity can occur within hours of taking a serotonergic drug, increasing its dose or adding another.

whyNot.1: Onset is much faster than 2 weeks.
whyNot.2: A month describes delayed effects, not serotonin toxicity.
whyNot.3: Six months describes long-term effects, not this acute reaction.

explain.body: Linked to all antidepressants, more often SSRIs, usually in older people and with diuretics. Consider it if someone becomes drowsy, confused or has seizures. Check sodium.

test.q: Which person starting an SSRI is at highest risk of hyponatraemia?
test.why: BNF and NG222 1.4.24: hyponatraemia occurs mainly in older people, especially with other risks such as diuretics.

whyNot.0: Young age is not a recognised risk factor.
whyNot.1: Exercise is not the named risk factor here.
whyNot.3: Smoking is not the named risk factor here.
